Hi Amit / Priya —

Thanks again for the time today — great conversation and really helpful context on the structured payouts and post-trade enrichment use case. Quick recap and next steps from our side: 

- Primary goals we heard: high JSON schema fidelity for downstream systems, <10% rejection on automated validators, and predictably low 99th latency for structured responses.
- Suggested immediate work: a focused model-fit eval (3 candidate models) + function-calling schema compliance tests + a small prompt set (~200 examples) reflecting your edge cases.

Recommended starting models (based on similar fintech workloads):
- redwood-chat-structured-1 (best for strict JSON output, lower hallucination)
- redwood-medium-v2 (cost-efficient, good for short structured completions)
- open-instruct-quant-8 (backup for throughput-sensitive batch jobs)

Attachments: please share your current sample schemas and a few representative transcripts (or drop in the Drive folder). I see Dev is cc'ed — he can share a lightweight eval harness and initial benchmark script.

Proposed next steps:
1) You share schema_samples.json + the Excel with labeled cases (you mentioned ~200 rows).
2) We run a 2-3 day sanity eval and return pass/fail per-schema plus a short quality report and latency numbers.
3) Technical deep-dive for integration and retry semantics (30-45m) — suggest Tue/Wed next week.

Does that timeline work? If yes, I’ll send calendar options and spin up an eval sandbox.

Thanks Marissa — this looks good. A few clarifying questions before we hand over the files: 

1) JSON schema constraints: our downstream validator is strict (reject on any unknown keys and type mismatches). Will your eval harness do strict schema validation (e.g., using ajv) or do we need to normalize responses first?

2) Retries / idempotency: for real-time API calls we expect a client-side retry with exponential backoff. How do you recommend handling duplicate calls that could cause duplicate downstream side-effects? Any built-in support for idempotency tokens in the function-calling flow?

3) Quality regression concerns: if we upgrade models (e.g., redwood-chat-structured-1 -> redwood-chat-structured-2), what guardrails do you provide to detect and mitigate regressions for our prompt set?

Hi Amit —

Great questions. Quick answers and a proposed technical approach we can run in the 2-3 day eval: 

1) Schema validation: we run strict validation as a first-class check. Our eval harness can run your provided JSON Schemas (we use ajv under the hood) and report pass/fail plus a diff for mismatches. We’ll include a small "normalizer" layer option if you want tolerated variations (e.g., coercing numeric strings) but default is strict.

2) Retries & idempotency: for function-calling / structured outputs we recommend the client attach an idempotency key per business operation. Redwood’s hosted API accepts an X-Redwood-Idempotency header which our runtime will surface to downstream logs and dedupe hooks. For built-in function-calling flows we also recommend enforcing side-effecting operations from your service side (e.g., check-and-insert guarded by idempotency token). We will include a sample wrapper in the eval harness.

3) Regression guards: we run release-diff style evaluations — you can supply a baseline model and a candidate; we compute schema pass rate, precision/recall on labeled fields, and qualitative regression alerts (examples where the candidate drops below baseline on key metrics). We can also tie to automated rollout (canary with auto-fallback) if you want to gate traffic.

Model picks & perf guidance (rough):
- redwood-chat-structured-1: schema pass ~92-97% on strict cases, median latency (~1.8s per response) for short payloads; best initial pick for fidelity testing.
- redwood-medium-v2: schema pass ~85-90%, median latency (~0.9s); good for throughput if you can accept slightly looser parsing or run a lightweight normalizer.
- open-instruct-quant-8: schema pass ~78-86%, very cheap (batchy workloads).

Implementation notes we’ll include in the eval repo:
- Ajv-based validator with example error buckets (type mismatch, missing required, extra keys).
- Function-calling wrapper returning {status, idempotency_key, diagnostics}.
- Retry strategy: exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 attempts for transient network/504s; permanent failures flagged for human review.

I’ll drop the eval harness link in the Drive folder and push a sample run tomorrow.

Thanks,

Hi all —

Following up with a few concrete engineering recommendations for the eval and production integration: 

- Deterministic structured output: use temperature=0 and top_p=0.0 for schema-bound outputs. Set max_tokens tightly to the expected output size to avoid trailing text.
- Schema enforcement: validate responses server-side immediately; on failure, run a single automatic re-try with a slightly adjusted prompt (explicitly ask "Return only JSON that matches <schema id>"). If still failing, fall back to a queued human-in-the-loop flow.
- Function-calling and retries: include an idempotency_token in both the function call payload and the downstream operation. Treat 5xx from Redwood as retryable; 4xx as non-retryable unless specifically a rate-limit.
- Observability: capture per-request diagnostics (model_name, model_version, prompt_hash, idempotency_token, schema_pass boolean, validation_errors). We'll add traces to the Redwood Console route you plan to use.

I've uploaded schema_samples.json with two example schemas and a small node.js snippet in the Drive folder. Link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1aBcDeF (see /eval-harness).

If you're open, I can run a quick smoke test on a subset of 50 rows tomorrow and share raw pass/fail + failing examples so you can see the typical error modes.

— Ethan
